name: Jojoba oil

card.summary: A sebum-like liquid wax used as a moisturiser and carrier oil; popular, but with little trial data.

quick.overview:
Jojoba oil is a golden liquid wax from a desert shrub, used in moisturisers and hair products.

Its sebum-like makeup is the main reason given for its use; trials specifically on appearance are scarce.
quick.mechanism: It forms a stable, occlusive layer on skin that reduces water loss, according to oil-comparison studies.
quick.risks: Rare contact dermatitis has been reported. It is not a food oil.

lead: Jojoba oil is a liquid wax pressed from the seeds of Simmondsia chinensis, a shrub native to southern Arizona, southern California and northwestern Mexico. About 97 percent of it is long-chain wax esters rather than triglycerides, which makes it unusually stable and slow to go rancid.[1][2]

People use it to help skin look softer and less dry, as a light facial moisturiser or carrier oil, and on hair and scalp to add shine and reduce dryness. It is a staple of moisturisers, shampoos and conditioners, and is often described as resembling human sebum, an idea that underlies much of its popularity with people managing oily or acne-prone skin.[1][2][8]

Published research consists mostly of reviews of plant oils for skin-barrier support, laboratory work and small formulation studies; trials that test jojoba oil alone for a cosmetic outcome are scarce.[3][4][5][6]

chain: Applied as a thin oil layer
Slows water loss and softens the skin surface
Skin looks smoother and less dry
angle.text: Jojoba oil sits on and in the outer skin layers and reduces water loss, so dry skin looks and feels smoother. Users also apply a few drops to hair and scalp for shine, or use it to dilute potent essential oils and active ingredients.

infobox: Liquid wax; melting point about 10 C

paras: Jojoba oil makes up roughly half of the seed's weight. Although it looks like a vegetable oil, it is chemically a wax with little triglyceride; its main fatty acid is 11-eicosenoic acid, with smaller amounts of erucic and oleic acids.[1] Unrefined oil is clear golden with a faintly nutty smell, while refined oil is colourless and nearly odourless.[1]

This structure is the reason the oil is described as resistant to oxidation and heat compared with ordinary plant oils.[1][2] Grokipedia adds that the shrub tolerates drought and heat and has been cultivated in arid regions of Australia, Israel and Argentina.[2]

The O'odham people of the Sonoran Desert used jojoba oil for sores and wounds.[1] During the Second World War the United States used it as an additive in motor and gear oils.[1] Commercial interest rose in the early 1970s, when collection from wild stands led to domestication of the plant.[1]

After the United States banned imports of sperm whale oil in 1971, jojoba oil became a substitute in cosmetics and industrial products, and it has since been used in place of whale-derived ingredients such as cetyl alcohol.[1] Because the plant grows slowly and is demanding to cultivate, the oil is typically used in small-scale cosmetic and pharmaceutical products.[1]

Jojoba oil appears in lotions, facial oils, lip balms and makeup removers, and is often marketed as natural.[1] Grokipedia describes it as non-comedogenic and hypoallergenic, attributing these properties to its sebum-like composition.[2] Reviews of plant oils for barrier repair discuss jojoba alongside olive, argan, sunflower and coconut oils.[3][4] One review of cosmetic oils describes jojoba as a moisturiser and conditioner.[8]

The oil is used in shampoos, conditioners and pre-wash scalp treatments, and traditional uses included promotion of hair growth.[6][7] A 2022 review of almond, evening primrose and jojoba oils covers their cosmetic applications in dry, ageing and juvenile skin, atopic dermatitis and scalp conditions.[9]

Because of its stability, jojoba oil is widely used to dilute essential oils and other actives. A clinical study in psoriasis used a jojoba oil-based nanocarrier to deliver the retinoid tazarotene, with the aim of reducing irritation.[10]

Microscopy and transepidermal water loss (TEWL) measurements have been used to compare how several vegetable oils and paraffin oil penetrate the stratum corneum and how well they occlude the skin.[5] Reviews note that the ratio of linoleic to oleic acid in an oil is thought to influence its barrier effects, and that processing methods such as cold pressing affect what an oil contains.[4] Jojoba's wax esters differ from the triglycerides in most oils, which is why it is often treated as a separate category.[6][7] Research reviews also report antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and antibacterial activity in laboratory settings.[6][7]

Toxicity studies summarised in a 2021 review and in Grokipedia describe low acute toxicity and minimal skin irritation, with rare cases of contact dermatitis reported.[2][7] Jojoba oil is not a conventional edible oil, and product labelling generally directs it to external use. A looksmax.org thread shows users asking about drinking it with peppermint oil for beard growth; replies from other members were sceptical, and no study of ingestion for appearance outcomes was found.[11]

No clinical trial was found that tests jojoba oil alone for acne, hair or ageing outcomes. Human studies that involve it include an observational pilot study of a clay and jojoba oil facial mask in people with lesioned skin and mild acne,[12] the tazarotene nanocarrier trial in psoriasis,[10] and a randomised trial comparing oils for perineal protection in labour.[13] Barrier and penetration work in volunteers compares several vegetable oils, including jojoba, using microscopy and TEWL.[5] A 1982 letter in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology discussed the oil in dermatology.[14]

timeline.event: US uses jojoba oil as an additive in motor and gear oils.[1]
US ban on sperm whale oil imports increases interest in jojoba as a substitute.[1]
A high-quality jojoba genome is sequenced.[2]

lore.intro: On T Nation threads and looksmax.org, jojoba oil comes up as a moisturiser for acne-prone skin and as a hair or beard oil, with its sebum-like structure as the usual explanation.[15][16]

claims.claim: Jojoba is 'very similar to human sebum' and tricks skin into producing less oil.
claims.believers: A T Nation poster on acne said a few drops after washing worked because the oil's structure resembles sebum.[16]
claims.experts: Reviews describe jojoba's wax-ester composition as distinct from triglyceride oils and often liken it to sebum; no trial was found testing sebum regulation in acne.[6][7]

claims.claim: Jojoba oil is a good moisturiser that avoids dryness from benzoyl peroxide.
claims.believers: T Nation users recommended it as a moisturiser and as a protectant when using acne treatments.[17][18]
claims.experts: Studies of vegetable oils show occlusion and barrier effects measured by TEWL, and reviews discuss jojoba among barrier-support oils.[3][5]

claims.claim: Drinking jojoba oil with peppermint oil speeds beard growth.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org poster asked whether taking a couple of drops in water was safe for this purpose.[11]
claims.experts: Jojoba oil is not a conventional edible oil, and no study was found of ingestion for beard or hair growth; reviews cover topical use.[6][7]

claims.believers: Folk use and cosmetic marketing link the oil to scalp health and hair growth.[6]
claims.experts: Reviews list hair growth among traditional uses; no trial of jojoba oil alone for hair growth was found.[6][7]
